principles.name: Economic empowerment
principles.description: Block's stated purpose: build tools that help sellers, consumers and artists take part in an economy that is open to everyone, including people the traditional financial system serves poorly.
evidence_signals: Connects own work to access or financial outcomes for real users, such as small sellers or underbanked people
Shows genuine interest in fintech, small business or financial inclusion, not only the brand
Considers who is left out by a design (fees, eligibility, accessibility) and acts on it

principles.name: Simple, powerful tools
principles.description: Make complex financial products feel simple for the user, while the system underneath stays correct, secure and reliable.
evidence_signals: Removed steps or complexity for users without giving up correctness
Prefers readable, working, well-structured solutions over clever ones
Explains the hidden complexity (failure modes, edge cases) behind a simple experience

principles.name: Customer empathy
principles.description: Understand sellers and consumers deeply, including their constraints (busy counters, flaky networks, tight cash flow), and measure success by their outcomes.
evidence_signals: Names a specific seller or customer segment and their pain
Talked to users, used the product, or watched real usage before deciding
Measures impact as a change for the user, not only as shipped output

principles.name: Kind, curious collaboration
principles.description: Rooted in Square's pair-programming culture: work closely with others, ask good questions, stay humble and kind, and keep learning.
evidence_signals: Thinks out loud and invites the other person into the problem
Disagrees on substance without being condescending
Shows a habit of learning new tools or domains quickly

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background, interest in fintech and Block's mission, logistics. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Technical screen (pairing)
rounds.notes: Live pair-programming in a shared editor, often a multi-part problem where each part builds on the last. Some teams use a take-home plus an extension interview instead. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Pair-programming coding rounds
rounds.notes: Usually two or three. Working, readable code and stated trade-offs matter more than the optimal algorithm. May include extending a partly built service. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: System design
rounds.notes: Often payments-flavored: point of sale, authorization, transaction pipelines, fraud. Correctness under failure (idempotency, retries, offline) is a frequent probe. Mid level and above.

rounds.name: Past project / technical experience
rounds.notes: Deep dive into a project the candidate built: decisions, trade-offs and results. Candidate reports call this the prior-experience or technical project review interview.

rounds.name: Behavioral / leadership
rounds.notes: Collaboration, disagreement, ownership, production incidents, customer impact.

rounds.name: Hiring manager
rounds.notes: Can come before or after the onsite. Scope, motivation, team fit.

rounds.notes: Reported for some roles and the APM program; may involve AI tools. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.notes: A/B test design, fraud and risk modeling, model evaluation in production.

rounds.notes: Metrics for Square or Cash App, metric diagnosis, growth questions.

question_patterns.pattern: A technical or product decision the candidate disagreed with, how they made the case, and how it ended
A complex production problem the candidate debugged or owned, from detection to fix to prevention
Something the candidate built that measurably helped a specific user or seller group
A decision the candidate made that others disliked or that rested on incomplete data, and how they handled the fallout
A project or product that failed, the candidate's part in it, and what they do differently now
How the candidate delivered with a small team or used automation or AI tools to raise output, and how they kept quality
Walk through a significant past project: goal, own role, key decisions and trade-offs, measured result
Why the candidate wants to work on payments, sellers or consumer finance, and what relevant experience they bring
Design a payment, authorization or ledger flow that stays correct under retries, timeouts and duplicates
Design a seller-facing system, such as point of sale or inventory, that keeps working through outages and syncs safely later
Detect fraud or risk in transaction streams: features, imbalance, latency, evaluation and the cost of false positives
Design and read an experiment on a checkout, onboarding or pricing change, including pitfalls like two-sided effects
Improve a Square seller or Cash App customer experience: segment, pain point, solution, success metric
A payments or growth metric moved suddenly; structure the investigation and decide what to do first
Choose and size the next bet for a Block brand (Bitkey, Afterpay, a new market) and how to measure it

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a technical decision on your team that you disagreed with. What did you do?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the decision and why it mattered (risk, cost, user impact). Show the candidate raised the concern early, stated the other side fairly, and used evidence such as a prototype, data or a design doc. Explain how it was decided and whether they committed fully once it was. Strong answers include a moment of changing their own mind or a respectful outcome either way. Pitfalls: silent compliance, going around people, or a story where the other side was simply foolish.

looking_for: How you disagree on substance while staying kind
Whether you commit once a decision is made
strong_signals: Raises the concern early with evidence
States the other view fairly
Shows the outcome and the relationship afterwards
watch_outs: Silent compliance or going around people
The other side was simply wrong

sample_questions.question: Walk me through a hard production issue you debugged. How did you find the cause and what changed afterwards?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Set the stakes: what broke and who was affected, ideally in money or users. Walk through detection, the debugging steps and the hypotheses ruled out, how the candidate communicated during the incident, and the fix. Then show prevention: tests, alerts, a runbook, a design change. For payments, mention customer remediation such as refunds or reconciliation. Pitfalls: luck as the method, blaming another team, or no follow-up.

looking_for: How systematically you debug under pressure
Whether you prevent the problem from coming back
strong_signals: States who was affected and how much
Describes hypotheses tested and ruled out
Adds tests, alerts or design changes afterwards
watch_outs: Found the bug by luck with no method

sample_questions.question: Tell me about something you built that made a real difference for the people using it.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Name a specific user group and the problem they had, and how the candidate learned about it (support tickets, user calls, using the product). Explain what was built and the choices made to keep it simple for the user. Show the measured change for users, and what was learned after launch. Tie it to access or financial outcomes where possible. Pitfalls: impact described only as features shipped, or no evidence users benefited.

looking_for: Whether you understand your users deeply
How you measure impact for users
strong_signals: Names a specific user group and their pain
Explains how you learned about the problem
Shows a measured change for users
watch_outs: Impact described only as features shipped

sample_questions.question: Describe a decision you made that was unpopular with your team or stakeholders. How did you handle it?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain the decision, the alternatives and why it was unpopular. Show the reasoning was grounded in user or business outcomes, that the candidate listened to objections and adjusted what they could, and that they explained the decision clearly. Describe the result and whether the decision held up; admit it if it did not. Pitfalls: pulling rank, or a decision that was not really unpopular.

looking_for: How you make and explain hard calls
Whether you listen to objections
strong_signals: Grounds the decision in user or business outcomes
Adjusts what can be adjusted after hearing objections
Says honestly whether the decision held up
watch_outs: A decision that was not really unpopular

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a product you worked on that failed. What did you learn?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Give context and why the bet looked right at the time. Own the candidate's part without blame, explain what signals were missed or noticed late, and how the team responded (pivot, shut down, fix). End with a concrete change in how they work, ideally shown in a later project. Pitfalls: a disguised success, blaming leadership or the market, or a vague lesson.

looking_for: Whether you own failures honestly
What you changed afterwards
strong_signals: Explains why the bet looked right at the time
Names the signals that were missed
Shows the lesson applied later

sample_questions.question: Pick a past project you are proud of and take me through it: what you built, the decisions you made and how it turned out.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Choose a project with scope that fits the target level and a clear personal role. Give a short overview, then go deep on two or three decisions: options considered, trade-offs, and why. Quantify the result and say what the candidate would change. Expect follow-ups on details, so pick a project the candidate knows thoroughly. Pitfalls: a team project with no clear personal part, or staying at the surface when asked to go deeper.

looking_for: Your own role and the depth of your decisions
Whether the scope fits the target level
strong_signals: Goes deep on two or three key decisions
Explains options considered and trade-offs
Quantifies the result and what you would change
watch_outs: No clear personal part in a team project
Staying at the surface under follow-ups

sample_questions.question: What experience do you have with payments or financial systems, and why do you want to work on them at Block?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Be concrete about relevant experience: money movement, ledgers, compliance, risk, or adjacent work with strict correctness needs. If there is none, show transferable skills and real curiosity about the domain. Link motivation to Block's purpose and products, such as helping small sellers or making money access easier, and to the kind of problems the candidate wants. Pitfalls: generic praise, crypto hype with no substance, or only compensation.

looking_for: Relevant or transferable experience with money systems
Genuine interest in Block's purpose and products
strong_signals: Names concrete correctness or compliance work
Links motivation to sellers or money access
Shows curiosity about the domain if new to it
watch_outs: Generic praise or hype with no substance

sample_questions.question: Design a point-of-sale system for sellers that can keep taking payments during a short network outage.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify scale, payment types and acceptable risk. Cover local storage of pending payments with unique client-side ids, a risk limit for offline acceptance (amount caps, card checks), and a queue that forwards payments when the network returns. Make the server side idempotent so replays do not double-charge, and handle declines found after reconnecting. Discuss encryption of stored card data, clock and ordering issues, and how the seller sees status. Pitfalls: ignoring duplicates on reconnect, or ignoring the risk of accepting offline.

looking_for: How you keep sellers working through failures
Whether payments stay correct after reconnecting
strong_signals: Uses client-generated ids and idempotent server writes
Sets risk limits for offline acceptance
Handles declines discovered later
watch_outs: Ignoring the risk of offline acceptance

sample_questions.question: Design a card authorization service that answers within milliseconds and stays correct when the card network times out.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify latency targets, volume and the parties (merchant, processor, network, issuer). Cover the request path, a durable record written before calling the network, and timeouts with a clear state machine (pending, approved, declined, unknown). For timeouts, explain reversals or status checks so no customer is charged twice or left with a hanging hold. Discuss idempotency keys, retries with backoff, partitioning, and monitoring of unknown states. Pitfalls: blind retries, or treating a timeout as a decline without cleanup.

looking_for: How you handle the unknown state after a timeout
Whether you design for low latency and correctness together
strong_signals: Writes a durable record before calling the network
Uses an explicit state machine with an unknown state
Uses reversals or status checks to resolve timeouts
watch_outs: Treating a timeout as a decline with no cleanup

sample_questions.question: How would you make payment requests idempotent so that a retry never charges a customer twice?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain why retries happen (client timeouts, network errors, user double taps). Propose a client-supplied idempotency key stored with the request and its result, with a unique constraint so concurrent duplicates collapse to one. Return the stored result on replay, and reject a reused key with different parameters. Cover key expiry, in-progress state and locking, and idempotency across downstream calls. Pitfalls: deduplicating by amount and time, or only checking in memory.

looking_for: Whether you understand why duplicates happen
How you enforce one charge under concurrency
strong_signals: Stores a client key with the result under a unique constraint
Rejects a reused key with different parameters
Handles in-progress requests and key expiry

sample_questions.question: Design a pipeline that reconciles daily settlement files from card networks against internal payment records.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify file formats, volumes, timing and what a mismatch costs. Cover ingestion with validation and raw-file archiving, normalization into a common schema, matching on stable ids with fallback rules, and buckets for matched, missing on either side, and amount mismatches. Make reruns safe and results auditable, and route exceptions to a review queue with alerts. Discuss late files, currency and fees. Pitfalls: overwriting data on rerun, or no plan for unmatched records.

looking_for: How you match records and handle exceptions
Whether reruns are safe and auditable
strong_signals: Archives raw files and validates on ingest
Defines buckets for each kind of mismatch
Sends exceptions to a review queue with alerts

sample_questions.question: How would you build a model to detect fraud in payment transactions, given that fraud is rare?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define the fraud type and label source, and note label delay (chargebacks arrive weeks later). Discuss features: velocity, device, seller and buyer history, network features. Handle imbalance with sampling or class weights and evaluate with precision-recall, not accuracy, at a threshold chosen from the cost of fraud versus blocking good customers. Cover latency for real-time scoring, rules plus model, monitoring for drift, and adversarial adaptation. Pitfalls: accuracy as the metric, or ignoring harm to legitimate users.

looking_for: How you handle rare, delayed labels
Whether you weigh fraud loss against harm to good users
strong_signals: Notes label delay from chargebacks
Uses precision-recall and a cost-based threshold
Plans for drift and adversaries
watch_outs: Ignoring false positives on legitimate customers

sample_questions.question: How would you design an A/B test for a change meant to improve checkout conversion?
sample_questions.strong_answer: State the hypothesis, the primary metric (completed payments per checkout start) and guardrails (refunds, fraud, seller revenue, latency). Choose the randomization unit carefully: buyer, seller or location, given network and seller-level effects. Size the test from baseline and minimum detectable effect, fix the duration in advance, and plan for novelty effects and multiple metrics. Describe how to read results and decide. Pitfalls: peeking and stopping early, or randomizing at a unit that leaks between groups.

looking_for: How rigorously you design an experiment
Whether you pick the right randomization unit
strong_signals: Sets a primary metric and guardrails
Sizes the test from baseline and minimum effect
Fixes the duration in advance
watch_outs: A unit that leaks between groups

sample_questions.question: How would you improve the Square point-of-sale checkout for small sellers?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the goal (seller revenue, speed, retention) and pick a segment, such as a busy coffee counter or a solo service provider. Map the checkout journey for both seller and buyer and find the main pains: speed at peak, tipping, connectivity, reconciliation at close. Generate options, prioritize by impact and effort, and recommend one. Define a success metric such as checkout time or transactions per hour, plus guardrails like error rates and refunds. Pitfalls: forgetting the buyer side, or features with no seller pain behind them.

looking_for: Whether you start from a specific seller's pain
How you prioritize and recommend one idea
strong_signals: Picks one seller segment
Maps the journey for seller and buyer
Defines a success metric and guardrails
watch_outs: Features with no seller pain behind them

sample_questions.question: Payment success rate dropped 5% overnight. What do you do on day one?
sample_questions.strong_answer: First confirm the drop is real (data pipeline, metric definition) and assess impact in money and sellers affected. Segment fast: payment method, card network, region, device, app version, seller type. Check recent releases, partner or network incidents and fraud rule changes. Decide immediate action, such as rollback or failover, and who to inform, including affected sellers. Then root cause and prevention. Pitfalls: a long hypothesis list with no order, or analysis before stopping the bleeding.

looking_for: How you structure a fast investigation
Whether you act to limit harm early
strong_signals: Confirms the data and sizes the impact
Segments by method, network, region and version
Rolls back or fails over while finding the cause
watch_outs: A long hypothesis list with no order

sample_questions.question: How would you get more Cash App customers to set up direct deposit?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify why it matters (primary-account relationship, engagement, revenue) and the current funnel. Segment customers, for example people paid by employers versus gig workers, and find where each drops off: awareness, trust, the setup steps, employer forms. Propose fixes such as pre-filled forms, early access to pay, or partial deposits to try it, and prioritize. Define the metric (share of actives with recurring deposits) and guardrails (trust, support contacts). Pitfalls: incentives only, or ignoring trust concerns about moving a paycheck.

looking_for: Whether you understand why direct deposit matters
How you find where customers drop off
strong_signals: Segments employees versus gig workers
Finds the funnel step with the biggest drop
Addresses trust in moving a paycheck

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Delivers well-scoped tasks with guidance; loop is mostly pair-programming coding with light design.
Owns features end to end within a team and writes working, tested code independently.
Senior engineer; owns services or systems, designs for correctness and failure, and mentors others.
Staff engineer; leads technical direction across several teams and large cross-team projects.
Senior staff; shapes architecture and strategy for a business unit such as Square or Cash App.
Owns features within a product area with support from a senior PM.
Owns a product area, its metrics and roadmap, working with engineering, risk and compliance.
Leads analysis or modeling for a product or risk area and influences product decisions with data.
Sets data and modeling direction across teams, for example for pricing or lending.

persona.tone: Friendly, collaborative and low-ego; treats the interview as working together, not a trick
persona.pace: Moderate; lets the candidate think out loud and builds the problem in steps
persona.pushback_style: Probes failure modes and correctness ('what if the network times out?', 'could this charge twice?') and asks how the user or seller actually benefited
persona.closing_style: Saves a few minutes at the end for the candidate's questions about the team and the work

case_style.notes: PM and data cases start from Square sellers or Cash App customers: product improvement, metric choice and diagnosis (payment success, direct deposit, checkout conversion). Payments mechanics and risk often come up. Market sizing appears mainly for new-bet questions such as Bitkey or a new country.

low_confidence_notes: values_framework: Block publishes no single values list for candidates. 'Economic empowerment' and 'Simple, powerful tools' come from block.xyz; 'Customer empathy' from prep guides; 'Kind, curious collaboration' from 2013-2015 Square engineering blog posts; A 'lean and accountable' value was considered from Feb 2026 restructuring coverage but left out, since it is not a Block-published value. values_share is set low at 0.2.

loop_structure: Cash App's official candidate hub pages now redirect to the jobs board and could not be read; round order and durations other than the one-hour pairing session come from prep sites and candidate reports, and vary by team. PM and data loops are thinly sourced.

bar_by_level: Block's numeric levels (L3-L7) come from levels.fyi URLs and forum posts; the mapping L5=senior, L6=staff, L7=senior staff is community opinion. The official career ladder PDF was not read. PM and data level names are titles from job postings, not an official ladder.
persona: inferred from Square's pairing-interview blog posts (2011-2015) and candidate reports; the process may have changed after the 2024-2026 layoffs and the move to smaller, AI-heavy teams.
scoring_weights: our estimate, weighted toward correctness, collaboration and user sense based on prep-guide themes; no public source gives weights.
case_style: no official PM or data case guidance found; the mix is our estimate from aggregated question lists.
sample_questions: most questions come from CleverPrep and TechPrep aggregations of candidate reports, not from Block itself.
